planting.note: Start indoors and transplant in late summer for a fall crop; Bilko carries high resistance to clubroot and Fusarium yellows, two soil-borne diseases that can persist in garden soil for years, along with excellent long storage life once heads are cut.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer for a fall harvest, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Bilko is a napa (Chinese) cabbage hybrid bred with high resistance to clubroot and Fusarium yellows, two persistent soil-borne diseases that can build up in garden soil where brassicas are grown repeatedly and have no cure once established. It forms tall, dense, barrel-shaped heads with crisp, sweet, pale green and white leaves well suited to stir-fries, kimchi, and salads. Beyond its disease resistance, Bilko is noted for holding well in cold storage after harvest, letting a fall crop stretch well into winter use. Cut heads when firm and full-sized, and keep soil consistently moist through head formation for the best texture.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Blue Vantage carries resistance to Fusarium yellows race 1 and tolerates excess soil moisture and tip burn better than many cabbage varieties, an advantage during the heavy rains common in Gulf South spring gardens.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Blue Vantage is a cabbage hybrid bred for resistance to Fusarium yellows race 1, a persistent soil-borne disease, combined with unusually good tolerance for excess soil moisture and tip burn compared to most cabbage varieties. It forms dense, round, blue-green heads that hold well in the field without splitting even after reaching full maturity, giving gardeners flexibility in harvest timing. Because it handles wet soil better than many cabbage types, it is a strong choice for the heavy spring rains common across the Gulf South. Cut heads once firm and full-sized, and use promptly or store in a cool spot for best quality.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Cheers carries high resistance to Fusarium yellows and intermediate resistance to black rot, and is notably resistant to head-splitting even in high heat, giving it flexibility across the Gulf South's spring and fall cabbage windows.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Cheers is a cabbage hybrid bred with high resistance to Fusarium yellows and intermediate resistance to black rot, two diseases that can persist in garden soil and spread through wet conditions. It is especially valued for resisting head-splitting even when hit by high heat or a sudden heavy rain after a dry spell, a common cause of wasted cabbage crops in changeable Gulf South weather. The round, dense, blue-green heads have good storage quality once harvested. Cut heads once firm and fully sized, and keep soil evenly moist through head formation for the best flavor and texture.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Rupp Seeds)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Bronco carries excellent resistance to bean common mosaic virus (BCMV), a widespread aphid-transmitted disease, and holds up well to shipping and summer heat, making it a dependable choice for a long Gulf South bean season.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Bronco is a widely grown commercial bush snap bean valued for excellent resistance to bean common mosaic virus, an aphid-spread disease that can stunt and discolor susceptible bean plantings, along with good heat tolerance and strong pod quality under summer growing conditions. It produces glossy, dark green, straight pods on an upright, high-yielding bush that needs no staking. Harvest pods young and tender, before seeds bulge visibly through the pod wall, and pick every couple of days to keep plants setting new flowers. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the warm season for a continuous harvest.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Rupp Seeds, Fruition Seeds)

common_name: Strike Bush Bean (Early Disease-Resistant Heat-Tolerant Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Strike is an early-maturing bush bean noted for disease resistance and a long harvest window, with good heat tolerance suited to a long, warm Gulf South growing season.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Strike is an early, disease-resistant bush snap bean prized for a long, sustained harvest window rather than a short, concentrated flush of pods like many bush varieties. It holds up well to summer heat, continuing to set new pods over an extended period when many other bush beans slow down. Pods are straight, tender, and best picked young before seeds bulge visibly through the pod wall. Harvest every couple of days to encourage continued flowering, and succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the warm season for an even longer supply of fresh beans.
sources: seed catalog reference (High Mowing Organic Seeds, True Leaf Market, Victory Seeds)
